title: Run your own image in the cluster
description: Get an image you built into the cluster with kind load or a local registry, then update it.

toc.text: 1.1 The quick way: copy the image into the nodes
1.2 The proper way: a local registry
Part 2 — Habits and gotchas worth knowing

html:
Get an image you built into the cluster and run it, then update it. Two ways: copy it straight into the nodes, or push it to a small local registry. This assumes the cluster from Create a local Kubernetes cluster with kind is running and the namespace web exists. The k3d version of the registry is in Create a local Kubernetes cluster with k3d.

#Part 1 — Run your own image

The problem. An image you build with docker build lives in your local machine's Docker. The kind nodes are separate containers with their own image store, and they pull images from registries on the network (Docker Hub and the like). They cannot see your local machine's image list. So kubectl create deployment my-app --image=my-app:v1 fails with ErrImagePull: the node looks for my-app:v1 on Docker Hub and finds nothing. Two ways to bridge that.

#1.1 The quick way: copy the image into the nodes

kind load copies an image from your local Docker straight into every node's image store, so no registry is involved. This walkthrough builds a tiny image of your own, loads it, runs it and updates it.

1. Make an image to work with. A folder with a two-line Dockerfile: nginx with its home page replaced:

2. Build it with a specific tag. -t my-app:v1 means name my-app, tag v1; the final my-app is the folder holding the Dockerfile:

3. Copy it into the cluster's nodes:

Check that the nodes now have it:

A line with docker.io/library/my-app and tag v1. (crictl is the node's own image tool; kind load put the image on all three nodes, not just this one.)

4. Run it:

Kubernetes finds my-app:v1 already on the node and does not try to download it. That is the default for any tag except latest. For latest (or no tag), Kubernetes always tries to pull, which would fail here. This is why the guide uses v1, not latest.

5. See your page:

In another tab:

<h1>hello from my-app v1</h1>. Stop the tunnel with Ctrl-C.

6. Ship a change. The node keeps the image it already has under a given tag, so re-loading the same tag does not update running pods. Use a new tag each time: rebuild as v2, load it, point the Deployment at it:

kubectl set image deployment/my-app my-app=my-app:v2 reads as: in Deployment my-app, set the container named my-app to image my-app:v2. (create deployment names the container after the image, here my-app, which happens to match the Deployment's name. If unsure, kubectl get deploy my-app -n web -o wide shows it in the CONTAINERS column.) Kubernetes replaces the pods one at a time. Repeat the port-forward and curl to see v2.

The sed -i '' form is the macOS one; on Linux use sed -i without the quotes.

If the pod shows ErrImagePull or ImagePullBackOff: the image was not loaded under that exact name and tag, or the tag is latest. Re-run the check in step 3 and compare the name with kubectl get deploy my-app -n web -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}'.

#1.2 The proper way: a local registry

A registry is a small container that stores images, like a private Docker Hub on your local machine. Build once, push, and every node pulls from it. Do this when you rebuild often or want to mimic a real setup.

How it fits together. The registry is a plain Docker container, not a Kubernetes object, so it is reached through Docker's own networking. No NodePort is needed.

Pushing the image (from your terminal):

  • -p 127.0.0.1:5001:5000 publishes the container's port 5000 on your local machine's port 5001 (loopback only, so nothing else on your network can reach it).
  • Because of that, docker push localhost:5001/my-app:v1 from your terminal reaches the registry.
  • A NodePort only exposes a Kubernetes Service. This container is not one.

Pulling from the cluster (from the nodes):

  • A node cannot use localhost:5001, because inside a node localhost is the node itself.
  • That is why the registry is connected to kind's Docker network, so nodes can reach it by name: kind-registry:5000.
  • Each node also gets a mirror file saying "localhost:5001 means http://kind-registry:5000".
  • So pods use the image name localhost:5001/my-app:v1, and the node quietly fetches it from kind-registry:5000.

Start the registry on port 5001 (restarts with Docker):

Put it on kind's network so the nodes can reach it by name:

Teach every node that localhost:5001 means the registry. Inside a node, localhost is the node itself, so each node needs a small mirror file. This loop does all three nodes:

What the loop does, line by line

kind get nodes prints the three node container names. The loop runs everything up to done once per name, with the current name in $node.

docker exec "$node" <command> runs a command inside that node's container. Here it makes a folder named after the registry address, localhost:5001, under /etc/containerd/certs.d. That is the folder containerd (the node's container runtime) reads for per-registry settings when it pulls from localhost:5001. -p means no error if the folder already exists.

Three parts joined by |:

  • printf '[host."http://kind-registry:5000"]\n' prints one line of text. It is the whole content of the file.
  • docker exec -i "$node" cp /dev/stdin <file> runs cp inside the node. -i keeps stdin open, so the printed line flows in through the pipe, and cp /dev/stdin <file> writes it to the file. (This is the trick for writing a file into a container without an editor or a shell redirect.)
  • The file is hosts.toml, in the folder from the previous line.

Ends the loop.

The file it creates has one line, [host."http://kind-registry:5000"]. Read it as: "for images from localhost:5001, connect to the host http://kind-registry:5000". It uses plain http, so no certificate setup is needed. Every node needs its own copy, which is why the loop runs three times.

This requires containerd to read that folder. If your kind version does not enable it by default, add this to kind-config.yaml before creating the cluster (the cluster must be re-created):

Prove it: push an image and run it from the registry.

Prints it-works. From now on, docker build -t localhost:5001/my-app:v1 . and docker push localhost:5001/my-app:v1 is the whole loop, and your manifests use image: localhost:5001/my-app:v1.

#Part 2 — Habits and gotchas worth knowing

  • Never use the latest tag for local images. Kubernetes then always tries to pull, and fails for an image that exists only on your Mac (ErrImagePull). A specific tag plus IfNotPresent, or a registry, avoids it.
  • Describe before guessing. kubectl describe pod <name> -n <ns> ends with an Events list that says what went wrong (image not found, no node fits, probe failing).
  • A Service is not a pod. port-forward to a Service needs a Service that has pods behind it. A Service of type ExternalName is only a nickname for another DNS name and cannot be forwarded.
  • Data is disposable. Pod storage vanishes with the pod unless you add a volume. Fine for a lab.
  • The cluster survives a Mac restart once Docker Desktop is back. If kubectl cannot connect, start the node containers again: see Part 2 of Stop, shut down and clean up.
